planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall onto evenly moist, humus-rich soil; seed needs a full winter chill and germinates unevenly the following spring as meltwater keeps the bed damp.

directions: Western valerian grows through the moist meadows and dappled margins of aspen groves across the central and southern Rockies, sending up a single leafy stem topped with a loose, flat-faced cluster of small white to pale pink flowers in early summer. The bloom carries a faint, sweetly musky scent typical of the valerian family and draws a steady run of flies and small native bees. Give it a shaded border or woodland-edge bed with soil that stays reliably moist through the growing season, since it collapses quickly in dry, exposed sites. Established clumps slowly thicken from a short rhizome and can be divided in early spring to spread the planting without disturbing the crown too much.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall on cool, moist soil under light litter cover; a full winter of cold, damp stratification is needed and emergence the following spring is sparse and staggered.

directions: Arizona bluebells colonizes the cool, leaf-littered floor of aspen groves across the Mogollon Rim, San Francisco Peaks, and southern Rocky Mountain ranges, pushing up soft blue-green foliage and nodding clusters of sky-blue, bell-shaped flowers soon after snowmelt. It fills the same ecological niche as its better-known northern cousin Mertensia ciliata but holds to lower, drier-draining slopes within the aspen belt rather than true streambanks. Plant it in deep shade to dappled light with soil kept humus-rich and evenly cool, where it goes dormant and vanishes entirely by midsummer heat. Mark the planting spot before the foliage disappears, since bare summer ground is part of this species' normal cycle rather than a sign of failure.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall onto moist soil and let winter cold stratify the seed; light aids germination, so scatter seed on the surface rather than covering it deeply.

directions: Tall mountain butterweed stands at the moist margins of aspen groves and the seeps and streambanks that thread through them, rising on leafy, often reddish stems well above most of the surrounding meadow growth before topping out in flat clusters of small yellow daisies from midsummer into early fall. Its height and late bloom make it a useful back-of-border anchor in a partly shaded, moisture-retentive native planting, where it draws butterflies and bees after many aspen-grove flowers have already finished. Keep the soil from drying out through summer, since this species naturally grows where runoff or seepage keeps the ground damp even in dry years. Cut the spent stems back after frost, as they otherwise persist stiffly through winter and can look untidy in a cultivated bed.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall on consistently moist, humus-rich soil; a full winter of cold, moist stratification is required and germination the following spring is typically slow and sparse.

directions: Small-leaf angelica grows in the moist, dappled margins of aspen groves and open conifer woods across the Great Basin ranges and Sierra Nevada, holding finely divided, fern-like leaves well below the airy white umbels that open atop slender stems in mid to late summer. It is a daintier, shorter-statured relative of the larger angelicas found in wetter mountain meadows, better suited to a woodland-edge herb bed than a bog garden. Site it in light shade with soil that stays cool and evenly moist, since it thins out quickly where summer sun bakes the ground dry. Allow a few seed heads to ripen and self-sow at season's end, as nursery-propagated starts are scarce outside specialty native seed sources.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in spring once the soil has warmed, or sow in fall for natural stratification; seed germinates readily without special treatment and plants often bloom the first year from an early start.

directions: Showy goldeneye fills the light-dappled floor and sunny openings of aspen groves across the Rockies, Great Basin, and southern Colorado Plateau, branching freely into a bushy mound covered in small bright yellow daisies from midsummer well into fall. It tolerates more light shade than most sunflower-tribe natives, making it one of the easier true-yellow bloomers for the broken light under an aspen canopy, and it keeps flowering on far less water than its showy display would suggest. Plant it along a woodland edge or in a lightly shaded dry border where competing growth is modest, since it can seed around generously in open soil. Shear plants back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage a tidier, more floriferous second round before frost.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall onto well-drained soil and let winter cold and freeze-thaw cycles settle the seed; germination the following spring is steady once snowmelt moisture arrives.

directions: Muttongrass is one of the few true bunchgrasses that thrives directly under an aspen canopy, forming neat, blue-green tufts across the dry, gravelly floor of aspen groves and open ponderosa stands throughout the Rockies, Great Basin, and Southwest. It cures to a soft tan by midsummer and stays attractive through winter, giving a shaded native planting structure that most showier wildflowers cannot provide on their own. Use it as a filler grass between taller aspen-grove perennials or along a dry woodland path, since it needs little water once established and resents heavy, waterlogged soil. Leave the old growth standing into early spring and simply comb out dead blades by hand, as mowing or shearing damages the compact crown.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and sow outdoors in fall so winter moisture and cold complete softening; germination follows promptly with spring warmth.

directions: Thickleaf peavine scrambles loosely through the leaf litter and open understory of aspen groves and dry montane woods from the Sierra Nevada and Great Basin into the Rockies, using short tendrils to lean on neighboring grasses rather than climbing aggressively. Clusters of pink-purple pea flowers open in late spring to early summer, feeding bumblebees early in the aspen-grove bloom sequence, and like other native peas it fixes its own nitrogen in poor, gravelly soil. Let it ramble along a woodland-edge bed or through a bunchgrass planting where it has low shrubs or grasses to sprawl against, since it looks sparse and leggy staked upright on its own. It dies back completely after seed set and resprouts from a woody rootcrown the following spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the crown while it is dormant.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall onto well-drained, lightly disturbed soil; a brief winter chill improves germination and seedlings establish quickly as a basal rosette before flowering the following spring.

directions: Drummond's rockcress colonizes the open, sun-flecked gaps and disturbed gravelly soil within aspen groves across the western mountains, sending up slender flowering stalks of small white to pale lavender, four-petaled flowers from a basal rosette in late spring. It is short-lived, often behaving as a biennial that flowers once and sets seed into long, narrow pods before dying back, so a planting relies on self-sowing to persist year after year. Give it sharp drainage and a lightly shaded, lean spot such as a gravel path edge or disturbed patch within a woodland bed, since rich or constantly wet soil encourages rot rather than vigor. Let a portion of the seed pods mature and shatter naturally each year to keep a self-renewing colony going.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall on well-drained, moisture-retentive soil and let winter cold stratify the seed; press seed lightly into the surface since light aids germination the following spring.

directions: Tall mountain fleabane grows along the shaded margins of aspen groves and the subalpine meadows that border them across the central Rocky Mountains, holding broad, slightly hairy basal leaves beneath single lavender-pink daisies that rise on upright stems through mid to late summer. It flowers later and larger than many of the low fleabanes found in the same aspen parks, giving a woodland-edge planting a long-lasting show of color once spring ephemerals have faded. Plant it in dappled light with soil that holds moisture without staying saturated, mimicking the seep-fed meadows at the edge of its native aspen stands. Divide congested clumps every few years in fall to keep flowering strong and to share divisions, since seed-grown nursery stock remains uncommon outside regional native plant sales.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
